subject: The New Rules For Big Tech's AI Spending

 Policy pointers: Warsh holds , but Bessent says future hikes not necessarily a mistake .

Top News
 
 
 
 The capex test 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
 An investor wanders into the house of three Big Tech behemoths while they are away. Our modern Goldilocks then sizes up their capital expenditures, finding one to be too hot, another to be too cold, and the third option "just right." A similar story is now taking place across the markets, as the artificial intelligence revolution spawns some new tales.

 Modern version: The bears returned with a growl after hours on Wednesday, with shares of Alphabet ( GOOGL ) tumbling 10% following a rare earnings miss . Capex reached $51.4B, while free cash flow swung to a deficit of $9.1B (from a surplus of $24.5B a year earlier), causing panic over the red ink and heavy AI-driven cash demands. Over at Microsoft ( MSFT ), the company is also looking to find the right porridge temperature. The firm just unveiled the largest voluntary buyout program in Big Tech history, aimed at slashing its global workforce by a quarter—again—with the aim of shoring up cash for its AI expenditures.

Amid all the chaos in the woods, there was a bright spot from a bear that had been in hibernation. Oracle ( ORCL ), which lost half its market value over the past five months, rebounded 10% yesterday following the guidance given at its Analyst Day. The tech titan finally got off its broken chair and assured Wall Street amid heavy concerns surrounding the spiraling cost of its AI infrastructure buildout. Positive free cash flow targets were announced , along with fundraising caps, peak capex horizon, and a long-term revenue outlook.

 Thought bubble: Cash concerns to fund the AI revolution also increased this week following Meta's ( META ) new $95B stock sale and the high capex warning found in Anthropic's ( ANT ) IPO filing. While the AI industry is still in the acceleration phase of spending, investors are demanding realistic paths to monetization and strong free cash flow. Those that spend too little on AI, or too much, are set to be punished, but a goldilocks scenario is likely in store for companies that get the recipe "just right." ( 2 comments )
